conclusion.label: leans_endorse

report:
**Conclusion:** The evidence generally supports the claim that opening a bedroom window improves sleep quality, primarily by reducing carbon dioxide (CO2) levels and improving indoor air quality. The evidence for opening a bedroom door is weaker.

**Key Findings:**

- A DTU study found that an open window improved bedroom air quality significantly, and that keeping CO2 below 750 ppm ensures air quality does not negatively affect sleep (https://www.dtu.dk/english/newsarchive/2023/05/ventilate-your-bedroom-at-night-you-perform-better-the-next-day).

- A field study in student dormitories showed that increasing ventilation—reducing CO2 from approximately 2,500 ppm to under 800 ppm through window opening or fan activation—improved objectively measured sleep quality and next-day cognitive performance (https://thelongevitystore.com/blogs/blog/the-ideal-sleep-environment-temperature-light-sound-and-air-quality).

- One study reported that 87% of participants slept soundly with the window open, compared to 70% with it closed. However, the same study suggested that opening the bedroom door alone may not improve air quality enough to enhance sleep (https://jewishreview.co.il/this-summer-trick-will-ensure-you-sleep-well-and-wake-up-refreshed-22702/).

- A review of multiple studies concluded that poor indoor air quality, including high CO2 levels in poorly ventilated bedrooms, is associated with poorer sleep quality (https://www.researchgate.net/publication/351687297_Reviewing_How_Bedroom_Ventilation_Affects_IAQ_And_Sleep_Quality).

**Summary:** Opening a window appears to benefit sleep by lowering CO2 and improving ventilation. Opening a door may help airflow but seems less effective than a window. Individual factors like outdoor noise, temperature, and pollution should also be considered.
